title: Computation of free energy profiles with parallel adaptive dynamics
correct_citation: T. Lelièvre, M. Rousset, G. Stoltz, 'Computation of free energy profiles with parallel adaptive dynamics', J. Chem. Phys. 126(13), 134111 (2007), doi:10.1063/1.2711185; arXiv:cond-mat/0611276 (v1 Nov 2006, v3 Jan 2007). https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0611276
note: I read the full arXiv v3 text, and every specific detail in the claim checks out. Selection is in Sec. IV.B: each replica trajectory is weighted by exp(int S(s, xi(Q_s)) ds), with S = c d_zz psi^xi_t / psi^xi_t (Eq. 25), where psi^xi_t is the instantaneous replica marginal. It is implemented with birth/death clocks in the SMC/QMC spirit (they cite Doucet 2001 and Assaraf 2000), and a killed replica is replaced by a copy of a randomly chosen one. The mean-field result d_t psi = (1/beta + c) d_zz psi holds for the modified overdamped dynamics (Eq. 22). The quote 'the convergence rate is still limited by the relaxation in each submanifold xi(q)=z' appears verbatim, as a theoretical remark with no experiment behind it. Model parameters match: 2D WCA dimer, N=16, rho=0.25, sigma=1, eps=1, h=20, w=0.7, beta=5, M=2000 overdamped replicas, dt=1e-4, reference M=5000 averaged over t in [5,10], indicator bins dz=0.05, 30 bins on [1.1, 2.55], time-regularisation tau/dt=100, c in {2, 5, 10}. Table III (c=10, K=50) covers M=1000/2000/10000. Comparisons use fixed physical time and fixed M; I found no equal-cost or wall-clock comparison. Three nuances the claim leaves out. (i) The error metric is the max-norm PMF deviation of the mean force averaged over K=100 realizations, a bias-type metric, not a per-run error. (ii) 'Especially early' is not uniform. At t=0.05, c=2 and c=5 are worse than no selection (20.4 and 22.9 vs 9.51). The big gains are at t=0.1-0.2, and at t=0.4 selection is still better (0.020-0.034 vs 0.066). (iii) Escape fraction (Fig. 2) is the other evidence.

title: Potential of Mean Force Calculations: A Multiple-Walker Adaptive Biasing Force Approach
correct_citation: K. Minoukadeh, C. Chipot, T. Lelièvre, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 6(4), 1008-1017 (2010), doi:10.1021/ct900524t (online 2010-03-04); HAL hal-00674607. https://enpc.hal.science/hal-00674607
note: Existence and metadata are confirmed via Crossref and HAL. The abstract sentence 'Diffusion along the RC is further enhanced by a selection mechanism, whereby far-reaching walkers are cloned, replacing less effective ones' and the deca-alanine test are verbatim on HAL. The Crossref reference list does include Doucet 2001, Del Moral 2004 (Feynman-Kac), Douc 2005, Kitagawa 1996 and Carpenter 1999. It also includes J. Chem. Phys. 126, 134111 (2007), i.e. LRS 2007, and Assaraf 2000 PRE 61, 4566, the same QMC reference LRS 2007 uses for its selection. New evidence beyond the claim: the Amber 2022 Reference Manual (Sec. 25.4, ref [597]) attributes the walker 'fitness function' and resampling explicitly to Minoukadeh 2010 (https://ambermd.org/doc12/Amber22.pdf). In that implementation w_n is proportional to exp(int S dt) with S = C Laplacian(rho)/rho, which is consistent with the LRS-2007 Laplacian source term. The full text was paywalled and the HAL PDF was blocked (Anubis bot check). So the exact fitness formula, whether rho is the instantaneous walker marginal or an accumulated histogram, the walker count, and whether any comparison is at equal cost all remain UNVERIFIED and second-hand. The claim already flags these correctly.

title: Multiple-Replica Strategies for Free-Energy Calculations in NAMD: Multiple-Walker Adaptive Biasing Force and Walker Selection Rules
correct_citation: J. Comer, J. C. Phillips, K. Schulten, C. Chipot, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 10(12), 5276-5285 (2014), doi:10.1021/ct500874p (online 2014-11-26), PMID 26583211. https://doi.org/10.1021/ct500874p
note: Existence and metadata are confirmed via Crossref, PubMed and Europe PMC. The abstract confirms: a multiple-walker ABF implementation in NAMD with walker selection rules; a short-peptide reversible-folding test; and, in transition-coordinate regions with hidden barriers, 'far more reliable results in appreciably less real time' than a single replica. I could NOT confirm the detailed claims. The full text is subscription-only: not in PMC, ACS paywall, no author PDF found. UNVERIFIED items: the weight w_i = 1/[C(n_t+1)]; the alpha=0.4 trigger (and the 0.2/0.8 results); the 2000/50000-step intervals; the <=10% overhead; 10 walkers and 0.1 A bins; the 12-32 vs 4-32 A results; 'best performer in the long-time regime'; and the quoted sentence about orthogonal degrees of freedom. Partial corroboration comes from the follow-up review by the same first and last authors: Comer, Gumbart, Hénin, Lelièvre, Pohorille, Chipot, J. Phys. Chem. B 119, 1129-1151 (2015), open at PMC4306294. It describes count-based selection weights (inverse of samples accrued since the last selection in a neighbourhood of bins) with resampling. Its switch-off threshold is 20% (not 0.4), and it says this weight is 'somewhat simpler than in previous studies'. In its deca-alanine test (16 walkers, 8 ns total) shared ABF plus selection gave the best short-time PMF, but all strategies converged to the same PMF at 128 ns. Overlap is plausible at the level of the abstract, but the specific failure-mode quotes cannot be confirmed.

title: Amber 2016 Reference Manual, ch. 22 (NFE module): multiple-walker ABMD selection algorithm and well-tempered ABMD
correct_citation: Amber Reference Manual (D. A. Case et al.), Free energies chapter, section 'Adaptively biased MD, steered MD, and umbrella sampling with REMD' (ch. 22.6, pp. 430-443 in the extract at https://ambermd.org/doc12/nfe.pdf, whose text says 'AMBER 16 introduces' WT-ABMD and walker selection); the same text appears in the Amber 2022 Reference Manual, Sec. 25.4, pp. 532-547 (https://ambermd.org/doc12/Amber22.pdf). The exact manual year of the nfe.pdf extract is UNVERIFIED.
note: I read the PDF pages directly. Everything in the claim is confirmed, and the weight formula the claim marked hidden is now readable. The weight is w_n = K^-1 exp(int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} S(xi_n^t) dt) with S(xi) = C Laplacian(rho(xi))/rho(xi). Key difference from LRS 2007 and from the project's step: rho is estimated from the ABMD biasing potential, which the manual calls 'approximately proportional to the histogram of the collective variable', i.e. an accumulated estimate, not the instantaneous walker marginal. Copy numbers come from W_n = floor(eta_n + N_w sum_{m<=n} w_m) - floor(eta_n + N_w sum_{m<n} w_m), which keeps N_w fixed, and coordinates and velocities are copied. Selection stops when the entropy of the weights drops below the epsilon threshold. C is called a 'pseudo diffusion constant': too large and all walkers become copies of the dominant one, too small and nothing is killed. Selection is 'most beneficial during the initial and middle parts'; late in the run 'it is best to proceed with the non interacting multiple walker algorithm.' The motivation explicitly names walkers 'bunched up' by hidden barriers along orthogonal degrees of freedom. It cites Minoukadeh 2010 for the fitness or resampling scheme (ref [460] in the extract; resolved as [597] = Minoukadeh, Chipot, Lelièvre JCTC 2010 in the Amber 2022 bibliography). This is a metadynamics-like adaptive bias (ABMD), not ABF, and there are no benchmarks.

title: Lambda-ABF: Simplified, Portable, Accurate, and Cost-Effective Alchemical Free-Energy Computation
correct_citation: L. Lagardère, L. Maurin, O. Adjoua, K. El Hage, P. Monmarché, J.-P. Piquemal, J. Hénin, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 20(11), 4481-4498 (2024), doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.3c01249; arXiv:2307.08006. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08006
note: Verified from the full arXiv v2 text, Sec. 2.4. Walkers run lambda-ABF independently and share mean-force estimates every 1 ps, with no selection. The sentence 'Although more complex multiple-walker strategies involving selection mechanisms have been proposed [69, 70], they offer only modest efficiency gains at the expense of increased computational overhead and implementation complexity' is verbatim. Refs 69 and 70 are Minoukadeh 2010 and Comer 2014. The abstract and conclusion credit both free lambda diffusion and multiple-walker orthogonal-space coverage for better orthogonal relaxation. Caveat: the 'modest gains' sentence is an unquantified assertion with no data or analysis behind it. Treat it as a practitioner opinion, not evidence.

title: Sampling rare event energy landscapes via birth-death augmented dynamics
correct_citation: B. Pampel, S. Holbach, L. Hartung, O. Valsson, Phys. Rev. E 107, 024141 (2023), doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.107.024141; arXiv:2209.00607. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00607
note: Verified from the full text. The paper adds Lu-Lu-Nolen birth-death to overdamped and underdamped Langevin. The KDE and birth-death rates are computed directly in the low-dimensional sampled space, and the authors assume the landscape U is known. The birth-death term drives toward the Boltzmann target pi, not toward a uniform CV marginal, and there is no ABF or metadynamics. It fixes the barrier-undersampling flaw of the original Lambda_0 term with a new term, Lambda_mu. Tests: a 1D double well with N=100 (barrier 4.3 kT, plus a sweep up to 32 kT where pure Langevin showed no transition), and 2D Wolfe-Quapp with N=1000 (N=100 in the SM). One correction: the baseline is pure Langevin with the same N and the same number of steps 'so that the same amount of statistics are used'. That is effectively equal force evaluations (KDE overhead ignored). What is missing is a comparison against fewer, longer walkers or wall-clock; they also study a birth-death stride M to reduce cost. The outlook explicitly proposes doing birth-death 'only in some relevant subspace ... of a few collective variables' as future work, which is the project's idea. They cite LRS 2007 and Minoukadeh 2010 as prior multiple-walker population methods.

title: TRR 146 Project A10: Population control of multiple walker simulations via a birth/death process (and APS March Meeting 2024 talk 'Enhanced Sampling using Birth-Death Algorithm')
correct_citation: DFG TRR 146 Project A10 (new), 'Population control of multiple walker simulations via a birth/death process', PIs B. Dünweg, O. Valsson, L. title: Free Energy Computations: A Mathematical Perspective
correct_citation: T. Lelièvre, M. Rousset, G. Stoltz, Free Energy Computations: A Mathematical Perspective, Imperial College Press (World Scientific), London, 2010, doi:10.1142/p579. https://doi.org/10.1142/p579
note: Existence, authors, publisher, year and DOI are confirmed via Semantic Scholar, the authors' CVs and many citing papers. Chapter 5 is the adaptive-methods chapter (cited as '[39, Chapter 5]' in arXiv:1008.3457). A Stoltz 2008 talk lists 'Selection procedures -> particle systems and jump processes' as a method class, which makes a selection chapter plausible. I could not access the book or its table of contents (World Scientific returned 403). So what Section 6.2.1.2 contains, and the claim that it suggests 'progressive reduction of the selection rate', are UNVERIFIED; that claim comes only second-hand through the paywalled Comer 2014. title: Free energy Sequential Monte Carlo, application to mixture modelling (Chopin & Jacob)
correct_citation: N. Chopin and P. E. Jacob, 'Free energy Sequential Monte Carlo, application to mixture modelling', in Bayesian Statistics 9 (J. M. Bernardo et al., eds.), Oxford University Press, 2011, pp. 91-118, with discussion by P. J. Green and B. M. Taylor. arXiv:1006.3002 (stat.CO, 15 Jun 2010). https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.3002. Page numbers are from Chopin's CV.
note: I read the full text on arXiv. The claimed overlap holds: the biased targets pi~_t have an approximately uniform marginal of xi on [x_min, x_max] and the same conditional given xi. The points the claim left UNVERIFIED are now settled from the text. (a) The bias is estimated adaptively from the current weighted particles: the incremental free energy D_t is estimated by ABP (weighted histogram of xi) or ABF (weighted mean force per bin), and A_t = A_{t-1} + D_t (Theorem 1, Algorithm 2). Sec. 2.2 says the target 'shall depend on a bias function which is estimated from the current particle sample'. (b) Uniformisation works through importance weights w ~ w_bar * exp(D_t(xi)). Resampling is systematic and triggered only when ESS < tau*N (0.8N in the examples). Each resampling is followed by adaptive Gaussian random-walk Metropolis-Hastings moves, and a final importance-sampling step removes the bias. With the ABP estimator the extra weight is about 1/(estimated bin mass of xi), so this is resampling with weights inversely proportional to the estimated CV marginal. It is a discrete-time relative of the project's uniform-target selection, but there is no continuous-time birth-death with a KDE log-ratio rate. Important differences: the 'time' is a data-tempering sequence (IBIS/annealing), not physical dynamics. The tests are Bayesian mixture posteriors (Hidalgo stamps with K=3, Iris), with no molecular system and no parallel-walker ABF dynamics. The example used ABP with 50 bins and N = 2x10^4 particles.

title: Computation of free energy profiles with parallel adaptive dynamics (Lelievre, Rousset, Stoltz)
correct_citation: T. Lelievre, M. Rousset, G. Stoltz, 'Computation of free energy profiles with parallel adaptive dynamics', J. Chem. Phys. 126(13), 134111 (2007), DOI 10.1063/1.2711185; arXiv:cond-mat/0611276 (v3 16 Jan 2007). https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0611276
note: I read the full text on arXiv (v3). Confirmed: Sec. IV B adds a selection step to parallel ABF/ABP with M replicas. Each trajectory is weighted by exp(int S(s, xi(Q_s)) ds), with S = c * d_zz psi^xi_t / psi^xi_t (Eq. 25). The paper says this duplicates 'innovating' replicas in insufficiently sampled xi regions and kills 'redundant' ones. Strictly, S is positive where the marginal is convex, so the rule is based on curvature, not on how far the marginal is from uniform. Killed replicas are replaced by a randomly chosen replica, and births overwrite a random replica. 'When convergence is reached, psi^xi_t is uniform and the selection mechanism vanishes.' Under the overdamped dynamics (22) the marginal obeys d_t psi = (beta^-1 + c) d_zz psi, stated as 'it can be shown', with no proof given. The verbatim sentence is: 'This method thus enhances the diffusion in the reaction coordinate space, but the convergence rate is still limited by the relaxation in each submanifold xi(q) = z.' It is asserted, not proved. Test system: 2D WCA solvent with a double-well solute dimer, N=16, density 0.25, h=20, w=0.7, beta=5, overdamped Langevin with dt=1e-4. M=2000 replicas, K=100 realisations, histogram bins of width 0.05 (indicator functions, not a KDE), 30 bins on [1.1, 2.55], parallel ABF (Eq. 20) with time-averaged conditional means (tau/dt=100). Table II (max PMF error): at t=0.05, c=2 and c=5 are WORSE than no selection (20.4 and 22.9 vs 9.51); c=10 gives 10.4. At t=0.1 and 0.2 selection is dramatically better (for example 0.035 vs 18.0). At t=0.4 the errors are about 0.026-0.034 vs 0.066. So 'lower error at later times' is supported, even though the text says 'especially at the early stages'. Caveat on 'more effective as replicas grow': Table III runs only c=10 at M = 1000/2000/10000 (K=50), with no c=0 control at each M, so the selection-by-M interaction is claimed but not isolated. The reference is not exact: it is an M=5000 run averaged over t in [5, 10].

title: Potential of Mean Force Calculations: A Multiple-Walker Adaptive Biasing Force Approach (Minoukadeh, Chipot, Lelievre)
correct_citation: K. Minoukadeh, C. Chipot, T. Lelievre, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 6(4), 1008-1017 (2010), DOI 10.1021/ct900524t (HAL: hal-00674607). https://doi.org/10.1021/ct900524t
note: Existence and bibliographic data were confirmed through Crossref, OpenAlex and the HAL API. I read the abstract only (ACS returns 403 and HAL is bot-blocked). Per the abstract, several walkers run in parallel and exchange information at fixed intervals. Deca-alanine convergence is 'globally improved through a more efficient exploration of compact configurations reflected in parallel valleys', and 'Diffusion along the RC is further enhanced by a selection mechanism, whereby far-reaching walkers are cloned, replacing less effective ones.' Nuance: the abstract credits the overall improvement to the multiple-walker scheme and credits selection only with further RC diffusion. It does not say outright that the force estimate is shared, although the 2015 review (refs 85 and 97) cites it for shared ABF. The exact weight or fitness formula remains UNVERIFIED. Indirect hint: the Amber 16 nfe chapter cites this paper ([460]) for its fitness-based resampling, and that chapter's rule is the Lelievre-Rousset-Stoltz exp(int C rho''/rho dt) weight. The 2015 review calls the 2007 and 2010 weightings 'somewhat' more elaborate than its own count rule 'while obtaining similar results'.

title: Multiple-Replica Strategies for Free-Energy Calculations in NAMD: Multiple-Walker Adaptive Biasing Force and Walker Selection Rules (Comer, Phillips, Schulten, Chipot)
correct_citation: J. Comer, J. C. Phillips, K. Schulten, C. Chipot, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 10(12), 5276-5285 (2014), DOI 10.1021/ct500874p; published online 26 Nov 2014, in issue 9 Dec 2014; PMID 26583211. https://doi.org/10.1021/ct500874p
note: Existence and bibliographic data were confirmed on the ACS page, PubMed and Europe PMC. I read the abstract only. It describes a NAMD modification for multiple-walker ABF, tested on reversible folding of a short peptide. It claims the multiple-walker strategy gives 'far more reliable results in appreciably less real time on parallel architectures, relative to standard, single-replica' runs, especially where hidden barriers slow convergence. This is a prior WALL-CLOCK claim for multiple-walker vs single-walker ABF, not for selection vs no selection, and is relevant to the project's Exp B. Caveat: 'walker selection rules' appear only in the TITLE. The abstract does not describe the weights. The rule the claim cites (weight = 1 / samples accrued since the last selection in bins j-h..j+h; switch-off when the min-max spread of 1/w is below 20%) is written in the 2015 review as 'Here, we calculate the weight...'. Attributing it to the 2014 paper is plausible (same lead author and code base) but UNVERIFIED from the 2014 text. I mark the claim supported only because it already flagged that the rule comes from the review.

title: The Adaptive Biasing Force Method: Everything You Always Wanted To Know but Were Afraid To Ask (Comer, Gumbart, Henin, Lelievre, Pohorille, Chipot)
correct_citation: J. Comer, J. C. Gumbart, J. Henin, T. Lelievre, A. Pohorille, C. Chipot, J. Phys. Chem. B 119(3), 1129-1151 (2015; online Aug 2014), DOI 10.1021/jp506633n; PMC4306294. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4306294
note: I read the Multiple-Walker Strategies section on PMC. Confirmed: selection rules 'eliminate replicas with values of the transition coordinate that are already well sampled, while duplicating replicas in relatively unexplored regions'. They are implemented by resampling with per-walker weights, and 'the selection mechanism automatically vanishes at equilibrium, namely when the biasing force is the mean force'. Weight = inverse of the samples accrued since the last selection in a neighbourhood of h bins around the walker's bin. Selection switches off when (max(1/w) - min(1/w))/min(1/w) < 0.2. The review says its weights are 'somewhat simpler ... than in previous studies (refs 48 = Lelievre-Rousset-Stoltz 2007 JCP, 97 = Minoukadeh 2010), while obtaining similar results'. Deca-alanine (Fig. 9A), all at 8 ns total simulated time: one 8 ns run is worst, 16 independent runs are better, shared ABF is better again, and shared ABF + selection is best ('almost indistinguishable from the converged one'). Exchange and selection happen every 20 ps. Fig. 9B shows 128 ns totals, and 'free energies converge to the same values for sufficiently long simulations, irrespective of the multiple-walker strategy'. Correction to the claim's 'no cost accounting': no quantitative speed-up is given, but the comparison IS at equal total simulated time (8 ns). It is a qualitative equal-budget comparison with no error bars or seeds reported in the excerpt I read.

title: Amber reference manual, Free energies chapter (nfe): ABMD multiple-walker selection/resampling
correct_citation: Amber 16 reference manual (2016), ch. 22 'Free energies', Sec. 22.6 'Adaptively biased MD, steered MD, and umbrella sampling with REMD', pp. 430-442 (bibliography pp. 898-899), served at https://ambermd.org/doc12/nfe.pdf. The year 2012 and 'Amber 12 manual' are WRONG: despite the doc12 path, the file is dated 2016 and says 'AMBER 16 introduces ... a selection mechanism for multiple walker ABMD' and 'From Amber16...'. The full manual's title and editors were not separately verified. ABMD primary papers: V. Babin, C. Roland, C. Sagui, J. Chem. Phys. 128, 134101 (2008); V. Babin, V. Karpusenka, M. Moradi, C. Roland, C. Sagui, Int. J. Quantum Chem. 109, 3666 (2009).
note: I extracted the PDF text through alphaXiv, so the claim's 'text could not be extracted' no longer applies. Confirmed: walkers 'bunched up' or clustered in a local metastable region 'because of hidden barriers that are oriented along orthogonal degrees of freedom'. Walkers in undersampled regions are cloned and those in oversampled regions are killed, with periodic fitness evaluation. The previously UNVERIFIED formula is: w_n = K^-1 exp(int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} S(xi_n^t) dt) with S(xi) = C * Laplacian(rho)(xi) / rho(xi). rho is taken from the ABMD bias, described as 'approximately proportional to the histogram of the collective variable'. This is exactly the Lelievre-Rousset-Stoltz 2007 Eq. (25) rule, ported to a metadynamics-like adaptive potential. Copies per walker come from a stochastic (systematic-type) rule floor(eta + N_w * cumsum w). Selection stops when the weight-entropy criterion E_w drops below -eps*log(1/N_w). C is described as a 'pseudo diffusion constant' (induced diffusion along the RC), and the manual warns that too large a C replaces all walkers with the dominant one. The manual says selection is 'most beneficial during the initial and middle parts' of a run. It cites [460] (Minoukadeh 2010) for the NAMD-script precedent and the resampling, and [437] (Lelievre et al. 2007) for multiple walkers. No dedicated primary paper for the ABMD selection algorithm is cited; implementers named are F. Pan and M. Moradi. That primary paper remains UNVERIFIED / not found.

title: Sampling rare event energy landscapes via birth-death augmented dynamics (Pampel, Holbach, Hartung, Valsson)
correct_citation: B. Pampel, S. Holbach, L. Hartung, O. Valsson, Phys. Rev. E 107, 024141 (2023), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.107.024141; arXiv:2209.00607. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00607
note: I read the full text on arXiv (v2). Every specific claim is confirmed. Lambda_0(f) = log(K*f/pi) - int log(K*f/pi) f has 'Lambda_0(pi) != 0 and hence pi is not a stationary solution'. With Lambda_0 'the barrier height is always overestimated', i.e. the barrier is undersampled. The fixes are Lambda_mu (pi replaced by K*pi) and the additive Lambda_ad = Lambda_0 - Lambda_0(pi). With Lambda_mu, undersampling appears only for very small bandwidth, and 'sigma_crit depends on the system and the number of particles' (SM Sec. S-IV). The stride study shows sparser birth-death is harmless 'as long as the birth-death events remain relatively rare'. At M = 10,000 steps, simultaneous events overshoot, with about 70% of particles killed or duplicated per step; this is a caveat relevant to the project. Both overdamped and underdamped (Bussi-Parrinello) Langevin are used. Equilibration speed is independent of barrier height for 1D double wells of 4.3-32 kT (N=100) and for a scaled 2D Wolfe-Quapp potential (N=100/1000). The outlook (pp. 15-16) proposes birth-death 'only in some relevant subspace ... of a few collective variables', with the CV distribution estimated 'on the fly ... by combining the method with collective variable-based enhanced sampling methods'. Key difference: all results assume the low-dimensional pi (energy landscape) is KNOWN a priori. The target is pi itself, not a uniform marginal, and there is no ABF or orthogonal degrees of freedom. For a uniform target on a non-periodic CV, K*pi differs from pi only near the domain edges, so the Lambda_0 bias they identify becomes a boundary effect for the project's rate.

title: TRR 146 Project A10: Population control of multiple walker simulations via a birth/death process (and APS March Meeting 2024 talk)
correct_citation: DFG CRC/TRR 146 'Multiscale Simulation Methods for Soft Matter Systems' (project no. 233630050), Project A10 (New): 'Population control of multiple walker simulations via a birth/death process', PIs B. Dunweg, O. Valsson, L. Hartung, https://trr146.uni-mainz.de/project-a10-n/ . Talk: A. Gopakumar Remanidevi, B. Pampel, S. Holbach, L. Hartung, O. Valsson, B. Dunweg, 'Enhanced Sampling using Birth-Death Algorithm', APS March Meeting 2024, session T18 'Advances in AI/ML-Driven Sampling for Atomistic Simulations', talk T18.2, 7 Mar 2024, https://meetings-archive.aps.org/mar/2024/t18/2/
note: The project page was read. Confirmed aims: a population-control scheme for multiple-walker CV-based enhanced sampling (metadynamics named as an example), adapting the Lu-Lu-Nolen birth/death sampler to molecular systems and integrating it into a CV-based multiple-walker framework. Motivation (verbatim): 'the multiple walkers' usefulness can be severely diminished due to walkers becoming correlated with each other'. Stated limitations (verbatim): 'It cannot describe higher-lying free energy regions as walkers there tend to be killed' and 'one must make sure that the initial distribution of walkers covers all the metastable states'. The page also calls birth/death exploitation-based rather than exploration-based. No funding period is given. The publication list runs to 2026 items, but the only birth-death paper listed is Pampel et al. PRE 2023. The talk exists with the authors above, but the abstract is truncated after its first sentence, so its content is UNVERIFIED. I found no paper or preprint combining birth-death with CV-based enhanced sampling from this group. Whether this is competing work, and what its results are, remains UNVERIFIED.

title: Accelerating Langevin Sampling with Birth-death
correct_citation: Yulong Lu, Jianfeng Lu, James Nolen. Accelerating Langevin Sampling with Birth-death. arXiv:1905.09863 [stat.ML], v1 23 May 2019 (only version; no journal-ref, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.1905.09863). https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09863
note: I read the full text. Every listed claim checks out. (a) Eq. (6) is Fokker-Planck plus the term -alpha_t rho_t with alpha_t = log rho - log pi - E_rho[log rho - log pi]. Thm 3.1 says it is the WFR gradient flow of KL. The WFR distance is defined with a mass-conserving penalty term (spherical Hellinger-Kantorovich). (b) Thm 3.3 assumes KL(rho_t0|pi) <= 1 and inf rho_t0/pi >= e^{-M}. It then gives KL(rho_t|pi) <= e^{-(2-3delta)(t-t*)} KL(rho_t0|pi) for t >= t* = t0 + log(M/delta^3), a rate independent of V. (c) Sec. 5, Eq. (14): Lambda(x_i) = log((K*mu^N)(x_i)) - log pi(x_i) - mean over particles. If Lambda>0 the particle is killed at rate Lambda and another particle is duplicated at random. If Lambda<0 it is duplicated and another is killed at random, so N stays fixed. Algorithm 1 (BDLS) says 'uniformly chosen from the rest'. (d) Prop 5.1 says only: if mu^N_0 converges weakly to rho_0, then mu^N_t converges weakly to the solution of the kernelized PDE (13) at fixed K. The authors call their proof formal (measure-valued generator argument). It has no rate and no bandwidth -> 0 limit. In the numerics h is hand-tuned, and choosing h on theoretical grounds is left to future work. (e) Birth-death acts on the full state x. There is no CV, marginal or free-energy estimation; the paper only cites Chopin-Lelievre-Stoltz in passing.

title: Birth-death dynamics for sampling: global convergence, approximations and their asymptotics
correct_citation: Yulong Lu, Dejan Slepčev, Lihan Wang. Birth-death dynamics for sampling: global convergence, approximations and their asymptotics. Nonlinearity 36(11):5731-5772 (Nov 2023). arXiv:2211.00450 (v3, 14 Aug 2023). https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00450
note: The venue (Nonlinearity 36(11):5731-5772, 2023) is confirmed by the UMN research portal, and other papers cite it as Nonlinearity 36(11):5731. I read the full text. (a) Thm 2.4: pure BD (spherical Hellinger flow of KL) contracts at a potential-independent rate from any rho_0 bounded below relative to pi. Neither an upper bound nor KL <= 1 is needed. Thm 3.1 gives the same for the chi^2 flow (BD2), which is the Lindsey-Weare-Zhang mean field, though with a longer waiting time, O(M) instead of O(log M). (b) The regularized energy is F_eps = int rho log(K_eps*rho) - int rho log pi (Eq. 32, following Carrillo-Craig-Patacchini). Thm 4.2 shows any minimizer pi_eps is O(eps) from pi in W2, under convexity/smoothness assumptions on V. Sharpness of the bound is only suggested numerically (Remark 4.3). (c) Thm 4.16: on the torus, smooth solutions of (BD_eps) bounded above and below Gamma-converge to (BD) on finite time intervals as eps -> 0. Unbounded domains are stated to be open. Thm 4.21 (torus): long-time limits of (BD_eps) converge to pi. (d) The particle jump process (Sec. 4.5) is linked to (BD_eps) only heuristically. There is no rate jointly in N and eps. Full state only. A detail the overlap text omits: the gradient flow (BD_eps) of F_eps has an extra term K_eps*(rho/K_eps*rho) - 1 in the rate. The plain KDE rate of Lu-Lu-Nolen 2019, which the project's rate resembles, lacks this term and so is not the exact gradient flow of F_eps.

title: Ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo with teleporting walkers
correct_citation: Michael Lindsey, Jonathan Weare, Anna Zhang. Ensemble Markov Chain Monte Carlo with Teleporting Walkers. SIAM/ASA J. Uncertainty Quantification 10(3):860-885 (2022). doi:10.1137/21M1425062. arXiv:2106.02686. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02686
note: The venue and DOI are confirmed on epubs.siam.org. I read the full text (arXiv v1). Confirmed: (a) Walker j is chosen uniformly, cloned and moved to z ~ q(.|x_j). Walker i is then deleted using importance weights, with an exact MH acceptance min(1, Z(x,z)/Z(x',x_i)). (b) The mean field (3.1) decreases chi^2(pi||rho), and its asymptotic rate is independent of the spectral gap of the underlying chain. After a time change (3.6) it is the Hellinger gradient flow of (1/8) chi^2(rho||pi). (c) The authors say the scheme 'cannot discover new modes any faster' than independent chains, and that 'the scheme enjoys rapid mixing once the modes of the target density have been populated'. (d) They write that 'the advantage from interaction tends to decrease as the dimension of the sample space increases relative to the number of walkers'. (e) Sec. 4 splits x = (u, v). An interacting move acts on u only: z ~ q(.|u_j), i is drawn with weights built from pi^(1)_{v_i}(.) = pi(., v_i), i.e. pi(u|v_i) up to a v_i-dependent normalization, which the extra factor pi_{v_i}(z) cancels. Then u_i := z and walker i keeps its own v_i. Independent MH moves on v follow. So orthogonal coordinates are not copied with the clone, the scheme is exactly pi-invariant, and there is no ABF or adaptive bias. CAVEAT on the overlap text's claim 'the only full-paper treatment of birth-death on a sub-coordinate found': this is a statement about the search, not about the paper, and it is contradicted by CV-space selection in multiple-walker ABF. Henin et al. 2022, Sec. 7.3.2, says: 'In the selection variant [226, 227], walkers are replicated or killed using a selection criterion that promotes undersampled regions of collective variable space.' The refs are Minoukadeh, Chipot, Lelievre, JCTC 6(4):1008-1017 (2010), and Comer, Phillips, Schulten, Chipot, JCTC 10(12):5276-5285 (2014). Per its abstract, Minoukadeh 2010 clones far-reaching walkers along the RC to replace less effective ones (tested on deca-alanine). I did not read the exact selection criterion. These are the closest prior art to 'ABF + CV-based kill/clone with orthogonal coordinates copied' and should be cited.

title: An operator splitting analysis of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao gradient flows
correct_citation: Francesca Romana Crucinio, Sahani Pathiraja. An operator splitting analysis of Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flows. arXiv:2511.18060 [stat.ML], v1 22 Nov 2025, v2 27 Feb 2026, v3 16 Sep 2026; no journal-ref. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18060. Log-concavity and decay results are now in: F. R. Crucinio, S. Pathiraja, Preservation of Log-Concavity and Convergence of Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Gradient Flows, arXiv:2609.18118 (16 Sep 2026).
note: I read the v3 PDF. The main overlap is confirmed. The paper studies Lie-Trotter splitting W-FR versus FR-W, with each sub-flow solved EXACTLY: no particles, no kernel, no discretization of the sub-flows. Order matters. With a suitable step size and order, the split scheme reaches pi faster than exact WFR in model time, at no extra cost in sub-steps (Prop 2.2/2.3 variational formulae). Prop 3.2 covers the Gaussian case: in 1D, W-FR is faster when C_pi > C_0 and FR-W when C_0 > C_pi, and in the multivariate case the mean offset also matters. Prop 4.2 gives conditions for W-FR acceleration on log-concave targets. CORRECTION on 'also shows WFR preserves log-concavity, with a sharp decay bound': this was in v1/v2, and the arXiv listing's abstract metadata still says so. But the v3 comment reads 'content from section 4 and part of section 5 has been moved to another arXiv submission', and the v3 PDF abstract no longer makes the claim. v3 proves log-concavity preservation only for the W-FR SPLIT scheme (Prop 4.1). It cites the exact-WFR bound J(mu_ngamma,pi) < J(mu_0,pi) e^{-ngamma(alpha_pi+1)} to [CP26], which is arXiv:2609.18118. The companion abstract calls its bounds 'explicit non-asymptotic convergence rates', not 'sharp'. Cite v1/v2 or 2609.18118 for that part. Full state; no marginal/CV operator.

title: Kernel Approximation of Fisher-Rao Gradient Flows
correct_citation: Jia-Jie Zhu, Alexander Mielke. Kernel Approximation of Fisher-Rao Gradient Flows. arXiv:2410.20622 [stat.ML], v1 27 Oct 2024 (only version; no journal-ref listed). https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20622
note: I read the full text. Confirmed: the paper links Fisher-Rao (Hellinger) flows, Stein flows, MMD ('MMD as de-kernelized Fisher-Rao') and kernel ridge regression. Thm 5.4 / Cor 5.5 prove evolutionary Gamma-convergence of kernel-approximated FR flows, but only the Gamma-liminf estimate, not full EDP convergence. The work is continuum-level with no finite-N rate. Caveats that weaken the stated relevance: (i) Their 'Fisher-Rao' is the Hellinger flow on POSITIVE measures without mass conservation. The spherical, probability-preserving version used in birth-death sampling is explicitly deferred to future work. (ii) Their kernel approximation regularizes the growth field by kernel ridge regression (K_mu + lambda Id)^{-1} K_mu delta F/delta mu with lambda -> 0. It is not a KDE/convolution of the density with bandwidth -> 0, and the authors contrast their approach with Lu-Slepcev-Wang's 'convolution and letting the kernel bandwidth go to zero'. So it bears only indirectly on whether a KDE-based birth-death rate approximates the exact flow. No marginal/CV.

title: On propagation of chaos for the Fisher-Rao gradient flow in entropic mean-field optimization
correct_citation: Petra Lazić, Linshan Liu, Mateusz B. Majka. On propagation of chaos for the Fisher-Rao gradient flow in entropic mean-field optimization. Proc. AISTATS 2026, PMLR vol. 300 (per PDF header); arXiv:2602.15094 [math.OC], v1 16 Feb 2026 ('to appear in AISTATS 2026'). https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15094
note: The paper exists and the venue is confirmed. The literal claims hold: kernelized interacting particle systems for the FR flow of F(m) + sigma KL(m|pi), well-posedness (Thm 2.9) and propagation of chaos (Thm 2.10, Cor 2.11). But the gloss 'i.e. finite-N particle error for kernel-smoothed birth-death' is WRONG on two counts. (1) The result has no rate. The authors write that 'Theorem 2.10 and Corollary 2.11 are non-quantitative, and obtaining convergence rates would require further work'. The result is lim_{N->inf} E[W_2] = 0, with no rate in N or in bandwidth. This settles the UNVERIFIED item: there is no explicit rate. (2) The particle system is not birth-death. Particles have FIXED positions and evolving weights (dw_i = -w_i a(mu~^N, X_i) dt, normalized to sum N), with no killing or cloning. The authors say they could not make the kill/replicate proofs of Lu et al. 2019 and Rotskoff et al. 2019 rigorous in their setting, because the flat derivative of KL is unbounded. Further limits: compact X only, pure FR with no Wasserstein/Langevin part (WFR with entropy left to future work), and an optimization setting rather than CV-marginal sampling. Sec. 3.4 also proves only weak-* convergence of kernelized minimizers. Cite it as qualitative propagation of chaos for a weighted-particle FR scheme.

title: Best Practices for Quantification of Uncertainty and Sampling Quality in Molecular Simulations [Article v1.0]
correct_citation: Alan Grossfield, Paul N. Patrone, Daniel R. Roe, Andrew J. Schultz, Daniel W. Siderius, Daniel M. Zuckerman. Best Practices for Quantification of Uncertainty and Sampling Quality in Molecular Simulations [Article v1.0]. Living J. Comput. Mol. Sci. 1(1):5067 (2018). doi:10.33011/livecoms.1.1.5067. PMC6286151
note: The metadata is confirmed. Verbatim checks: 'authors should report (and graph) their best estimates of 95% confidence intervals' (for fields without a reporting standard). The checklist says 'Consider multiple runs instead of a single simulation.' 'report a complete description of your uncertainty quantification procedure, detailed enough to permit reproduction of reported findings.' Small location and wording fixes: the quote 'multiple, potentially correlated trajectories within a single enhanced-sampling simulation ... can invalidate the assumptions underpinning traditional analyses of uncertainty' is in the Best Practices Checklist (Sec. 2), which points to Sec. 8 ('Assessing Uncertainty in Enhanced Sampling Simulations'). It is not in Sec. 8 itself. The Sec. 8 wording is 'consider taking a "bottom line" approach, and assessing sampling based on multiple independent runs'. The word 'safest' appears only in Sec. 8.2 (Weighted Ensemble): 'the safest way to assess uncertainty in WE simulations is to run multiple instances'. That section also says 'the variance computed in an observable from multiple runs should be based on values at the same time point'. Three statements are the project's own reasonable inferences, not text in the paper: the seed, not the walker, is the unit of replication; FR clones share ancestry; errors should be compared at matched cost.

title: Enhanced Sampling Methods for Molecular Dynamics Simulations [Article v1.0]
correct_citation: Jérôme Hénin, Tony Lelièvre, Michael R. Shirts, Omar Valsson, Lucie Delemotte. Enhanced Sampling Methods for Molecular Dynamics Simulations [Article v1.0]. Living J. Comput. Mol. Sci. 4(1):1583 (2022; published 2022-12-14). doi:10.33011/livecoms.4.1.1583. arXiv:2202.04164 (v2 25 Aug 2022). https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04164
note: The metadata is confirmed on livecomsjournal.org. I retrieved the full Sec. 1.3. The list has THREE bullets: efficiency depends on 'the application; the choice of parameters—and the optimal parameters are themselves application dependent; the expertise of the user.' The section continues that a fair comparison needs 'a benchmark for which the results are known to a high accuracy and precision', with each method used 'fairly', i.e. 'either using the optimal parameters for the particular application, or the best parameters that a typical user will be able to set in practice'. So the earlier UNVERIFIED tail is now resolved. The same section adds caveats a reviewer could turn against the project. Ground truth is 'seldom known beyond simple systems such as alanine dipeptide', with 'no guarantee' of transfer to complex systems. And 'a method may be less efficient than another when used optimally, but more robust to non-optimal circumstances.' The multiple-walker metadynamics passage (Sec. 7.2.1) is confirmed verbatim: 'A way to reduce the wall-clock time for convergence and make a better usage of modern parallel HPC resources is to employ multiple walkers or replicas'. IMPORTANT OMISSION: Sec. 7.3.2 (Multiple-walker ABF) says 'In the selection variant [226, 227], walkers are replicated or killed using a selection criterion that promotes undersampled regions of collective variable space.' The refs are Minoukadeh, Chipot, Lelievre, JCTC 6:1008 (2010), and Comer et al., JCTC 10:5276 (2014). This is direct prior art for ABF plus CV-based kill/clone, and it must be cited and contrasted. Another possibly related work, UNVERIFIED as to CV/marginal use: Pampel, Holbach, Hartung, Valsson, 'Sampling rare event energy landscapes via birth-death augmented dynamics', Phys. Rev. E 107, 024141 (2023), arXiv:2209.00607. It modifies the Lu-Lu-Nolen kernel approximation to fix barrier-region sampling and proves convergence still holds. I did not check whether it acts on a CV.

title: A Second Look at Canonical Sampling of Biomolecules using Replica Exchange Simulation
correct_citation: D. M. Zuckerman, E. Lyman, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2006, 2(4), 1200-1202, doi:10.1021/ct0600464 (Crossref confirms issue 4); arXiv:physics/0601145. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0601145
note: Bibliographic details confirmed through Crossref. The arXiv page itself carries no journal reference. I read the full text on ar5iv. Obs. I says that instead of REMD 'one has the option of running an ordinary parallel simulation at T0 ... or even M independent simulations'. The paper says 'A truly efficient method must be a superior alternative to such brute force simulation', and that otherwise REMD does not 'break even' in total CPU cost. The paper also states: 'Another claim of efficiency, by Duan and coworkers [7], fails to include the full CPU cost of all M levels.' Ref. 7 is Zhang, Wu and Duan 2005. Roe et al. are faulted for the same omission. One wording fix: (M+1)×t_sim is the cost of the REMD ladder (M+1 levels). The brute-force benchmark in Obs. III runs 'for the full length M×t_sim'. The paper is about temperature REMD for canonical sampling, not ABF or walker selection. Its use as the standard a reviewer would apply to the project is the claimant's analogy, but the analogy is fair.

title: How Efficient Is Replica Exchange Molecular Dynamics? An Analytic Approach
correct_citation: H. Nymeyer, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2008, 4(4), 626-636, doi:10.1021/ct7003337 (Crossref confirmed; online 2008-03-15). https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ct7003337
note: Abstract read on ACS. It supports the claim: 'Choosing the maximum temperature too high can result in REMD becoming significantly less efficient than conventional MD.' It also says 'the number of replicas in REMD, while important for simulations shorter than one or two relaxation times, has a minimal effect on the asymptotic efficiency of the method.' Two things the claim leaves out. First, the headline finding is favourable to REMD: 'as long as there is a positive activation energy for folding, REMD is more efficient than MD.' Second, the 'number of replicas' means rungs of a temperature ladder, not parallel walkers on a reaction coordinate. The parallel to FR's large-N, short-time gains is therefore the claimant's analogy. Nothing in the paper speaks to ABF.

title: Efficient reconstruction of complex free energy landscapes by multiple walkers metadynamics
correct_citation: P. Raiteri, A. Laio, F. L. Gervasio, C. Micheletti, M. Parrinello, J. Phys. Chem. B 2006, 110(8), 3533-3539, doi:10.1021/jp054359r (Crossref confirmed; online 2005-10-28). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16494409
note: Abstract confirmed on the SISSA (Micheletti) page. It reads: 'We show that the error on the reconstructed free energy does not depend on the number of walkers, leading to a fully linear scaling algorithm even on inexpensive loosely coupled clusters of PCs.' The PubMed page itself did not render (cookie wall), so the PMID is not independently checked, though the DOI is. The claim reads this as a time-to-solution gain at roughly equal aggregate cost, not a saving in total compute. That reading follows from 'linear scaling' but is an inference: I did not read the full text to see at what total simulated time the error was held fixed. The paper also combines multiple-walker metadynamics with WHAM. It involves no walker selection or birth-death.

title: Computation of free energy profiles with parallel adaptive dynamics
correct_citation: T. Lelièvre, M. Rousset, G. Stoltz, J. Chem. Phys. 2007, 126(13), 134111, doi:10.1063/1.2711185 (Crossref confirmed); arXiv:cond-mat/0611276. https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0611276
note: Confirmed, and the model system the claim left UNVERIFIED is now resolved from the full text (ar5iv). It is a 2D periodic box of N=16 particles with the purely repulsive WCA pair potential (sigma=epsilon=1, density 0.25). Two of the particles form a solute dimer whose WCA interaction is replaced by a double-well potential V_S(r) with compact and stretched minima. The reaction coordinate is the dimer bond length and beta=5. So the paper's test case is indeed a WCA-solvated bistable dimer. Whether it matches the project's WCA parameters I did not check (no repo reads). Selection mechanism: a jump process weights each replica by exp(int S dt), with source term S = c ∂_zz ψ^ξ_t / ψ^ξ_t (c=10 in the main runs). Here ψ^ξ_t is the replicas' marginal density on the reaction coordinate. A dead replica is replaced by a randomly chosen one, i.e. orthogonal coordinates are copied. It is birth-death on the reaction-coordinate marginal, the same family as marginal FR, but not a uniform-target FR rate. Evidence basis: selection on vs off at the same number of replicas (M=2000), the same time (t=0.1) and K=100 realizations. A second test varies M from 1000 to 10000 at c=10, with no no-selection baseline. There is NO equal-total-compute comparison against fewer replicas run for longer. This is exactly the 'same large N' kind of evidence the project already has. The paper concludes 'the selection process improves the rate of convergence of the algorithm.'

title: Potential of Mean Force Calculations: A Multiple-Walker Adaptive Biasing Force Approach
correct_citation: K. Minoukadeh, C. Chipot, T. Lelièvre, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2010, 6(4), 1008-1017, doi:10.1021/ct900524t (ACS + HAL hal-00674607; online 2010-03-04, issue 2010-04-13). https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ct900524t
note: Abstract confirmed on ACS and HAL. It describes multiple walkers in parallel 'exchanging information at fixed intervals'. On deca-alanine it reports convergence 'globally improved through a more efficient exploration of compact configurations'. It states: 'Diffusion along the RC is further enhanced by a selection mechanism, whereby far-reaching walkers are cloned, replacing less effective ones.' Everything the claim asserts from the abstract is supported. Still UNVERIFIED: whether efficiency was judged at equal aggregate time, and the exact selection rule. The HAL full text is behind bot protection and ACS is paywalled. Note that this rule rewards how far a walker has travelled. It is not a density-balancing or uniform-target rule, unlike the 2014 and 2015 Chipot-group rules.

title: Multiple-Replica Strategies for Free-Energy Calculations in NAMD: Multiple-Walker Adaptive Biasing Force and Walker Selection Rules
correct_citation: J. Comer, J. C. Phillips, K. Schulten, C. Chipot, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2014, 10(12), 5276-5285, doi:10.1021/ct500874p (published 2014-11-14). https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ct500874p
note: PARTIAL. The abstract quote is verbatim correct. But I read the full text (author PDF at ks.uiuc.edu), and it undercuts the claim's inference that the field credits walker selection by real time. (1) The paper explicitly compares strategies 'in terms of both real time and computational cost'. The Fig. 4 comparisons are 'based on similar computational cost': a 12 ns single walker vs 10 walkers × 1.2 ns. On 12-32 Å, multiple walkers give similar or better accuracy at equal cost and about one-tenth the real time. On 4-32 Å, multiple-walker ABF 'also reduces the computational cost'. (2) The selection rules specifically show 'adverse effects over longer simulation times'. Multiple-walker ABF WITHOUT selection is 'the best performer in the long-time regime'. The authors recommend applying selection only early, then switching to plain shared ABF. (3) The rule is count-based: weight = 1/(n_t(bin)+1) with cumulative bin counts. Selection is disabled when (max-min)/max < alpha (alpha=0.4). The authors state that 'the selection rules do not take into account sampling along orthogonal degrees of freedom'. The test system is deca-alanine in vacuum, end-to-end distance, 10 walkers. This is directly relevant prior art for both the project's equal-cost standard and its finding that early or uniform selection can hurt later.

title: The Adaptive Biasing Force Method: Everything You Always Wanted To Know but Were Afraid To Ask
correct_citation: J. Comer, J. C. Gumbart, J. Hénin, T. Lelièvre, A. Pohorille, C. Chipot, J. Phys. Chem. B 2015, 119(3), 1129-1151, doi:10.1021/jp506633n (Crossref; online 2014-09-23). https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jp506633n
note: Verified from the ACS full-text page and the HAL copy. The review says verbatim: 'These selection rules eliminate replicas with values of the transition coordinate that are already well sampled, while duplicating replicas in relatively unexplored regions, enforcing more uniform sampling.' It continues: 'The basic requirement is that the selection mechanism automatically vanishes at equilibrium.' And: 'The weight assigned to each walker is the inverse of the number of samples accrued in a neighborhood of bins near the walker', using n_j(t) - n_j(t_last), the counts since the last selection, over ±h bins. Selection is 'switched off when the smallest and largest n_i(t) differ by less than 20%'. Deca-alanine, Fig. 9A, 8 ns total simulated time: 'single' (one 8 ns run), 'independent' (16 walkers × 0.5 ns), 'shared', and 'selection' (synchronised and selected every 20 ps). Fig. 9B at 128 ns total shows that 'the free energies converge to the same values for sufficiently long simulations, irrespective of the multiple-walker strategy.' Minor caveats: the review does not explicitly say that orthogonal coordinates are copied on cloning (implied by replica resampling; the 2014 JCTC paper states it). The claim that count-balancing ties marginal FR on WCA is project-internal and not checkable here.

title: Accelerating Molecular Dynamics Simulations with Population Annealing
correct_citation: H. Christiansen, M. Weigel, W. Janke, Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 060602 (2019), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.060602; arXiv:1806.06016. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.060602
note: PARTIAL. Verified from the abstract and full text (arXiv HTML and the author PDF). The method follows a population 'while periodically replicating particularly well equilibrated copies (reminiscent of go with the winners strategies)'. It is 'found to yield similar performance for the same computational resources' as parallel tempering, and 'scales to a nearly arbitrary number of parallel processors'. The paper also states that 'the scaling efficiency S_p/p is consistently high and never drops below 85%'. One sub-claim is WRONG: strong and weak scaling are NOT reported separately. Fig. 6 shows a single series: fixed population R=10,000, theta=4375, cores p varied. The authors label it 'weak scaling', although in standard usage a fixed problem size is strong scaling. The other scenario, with population growing with resources, which they call 'strong scaling', is only asserted to be 'even better', citing work 'in preparation'. Also, PA resamples by Boltzmann reweighting between temperature steps, not toward a target marginal on a CV. The test system is met-enkephalin. The paper is a valid template for publishing equal-cost parity plus a scaling result, but it supplies only one measured scaling curve.

title: Weighted Ensemble Simulation: Review of Methodology, Applications, and Software
correct_citation: Zuckerman DM, Chong LT. Weighted Ensemble Simulation: Review of Methodology, Applications, and Software. Annu. Rev. Biophys. 46:43-57 (2017). doi:10.1146/annurev-biophys-070816-033834. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5896317
note: The citation is correct as given. Most of the overlap claim checks out, with two qualifications. VERIFIED QUOTES (PMC full text, 'Error and Efficiency Analysis' section): 'the efficiency of WE has been determined by considering the aggregate simulation time that has been required to yield the same rate constant and corresponding statistical precision as the standard simulations'. The same section also says efficiency 'is best assessed relative to standard parallelized simulations as the gold standard'. SUPERLINEAR: the paper gives no formal definition. The abstract says WE 'can achieve superlinear scaling—the unbiased estimation of key observables such as rate constants and equilibrium state populations to greater precision than would be possible with ordinary parallel simulation'. The Applications section adds that observables 'can be estimated with orders of magnitude fewer overall computing resources compared to standard parallelized simulations'. So reading it as 'more precision than ordinary parallel simulation at the same aggregate cost' is a fair paraphrase, but the abstract does not state the equal-cost condition explicitly. NOT SUPPORTED: the paper never calls WE 'the most established' kill/clone method. It says WE was 'one of the first rare-events methods introduced for molecular systems' and that the splitting idea 'has been rediscovered numerous times'. That characterization should be dropped or attributed to the authors. Also, the efficiency rule is stated for rate constants and pathway counts, not free energies. Applying it to FR-ABF is the project's own inference.

title: Optimizing weighted ensemble sampling of steady states
correct_citation: Aristoff D, Zuckerman DM. Optimizing Weighted Ensemble Sampling of Steady States. Multiscale Model. Simul. 18(2):646-673 (2020). doi:10.1137/18M1212100. arXiv:1806.00860 (v1 3 Jun 2018 ... v5 20 Apr 2020). https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00860
note: The work exists, and the journal venue that was marked UNVERIFIED is now confirmed via Crossref and the arXiv journal-ref: SIAM Multiscale Model. Simul. 18(2), 646-673 (2020). VERSION CAVEAT on the 'ad hoc rule' quote: the phrase appears only in earlier arXiv versions. v3 (8 Jun 2019, Aristoff & Zuckerman) reads 'Traditionally, WE refers to resampling based on an ad hoc rule: maintaining a roughly spatially uniform distribution of replicas in the bins.' v1 (3 Jun 2018) was by Aristoff alone, under a different title ('Optimizing weighted ensemble sampling for steady states and rare events'), and reads '...an ad hoc rule: maintaining a roughly uniform distribution of replicas.' The published version (v5 / MMS) drops this sentence. Its abstract only says the new strategies are compared 'with more traditional ones'. In the introduction, 'ad hoc' is applied to BIN choice, not allocation: 'In most weighted ensemble simulations, and in [5], bins are chosen in an ad hoc way.' The quote should therefore be cited to arXiv:1806.00860v3, not the journal version. SUPPORTED: the published abstract says 'We derive, from first principles, strategies for optimizing ... the number of replicas to maintain in each bin'. Eq. 4.4 gives the allocation that minimizes mutation variance, N(u) proportional to sqrt(w(u) * sum w_i Var_K h), and Fig. 6.4 shows optimized allocation beating 'uniform allocation' (particles spread evenly among occupied bins). Scope: the optimality is for the variance of a steady-state average (a mean first passage time via the Hill relation) in a 1-D toy problem with weighted resampling, not for free-energy/ABF error. The parallel to 'adequate rather than equal per-bin counts' is the project's own analogy.

title: Accelerating Langevin Sampling with Birth-death
correct_citation: Lu Y, Lu J, Nolen J. Accelerating Langevin Sampling with Birth-death. arXiv:1905.09863 [stat.ML] (2019). No journal-ref on arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09863
note: The work exists: arXiv v1 submitted 23 May 2019, with no journal reference on arXiv. The Duke Scholars entry names no venue, and I found no journal publication, so treat it as a preprint. VERIFIED FROM THE PDF: the mean-field PDE is overdamped Fokker-Planck plus a nonlocal birth-death term (eq. 1/6). Theorem 3.1 shows it is the gradient flow of KL(.|pi) under a (mass-conserving) Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao distance. Theorem 3.3 gives an asymptotic convergence rate independent of the potential barrier, after a waiting time and under a lower-bound condition. The particle scheme (eq. 13-14, Algorithm 1 'BDLS') uses a kernel-mollified density log(K*mu^N), with a Gaussian kernel whose width h is 'tuned to produce the best numerical performance'. Evidence consists of two analytic examples (uniform measure on a torus, double well) and toy numerics (four-mode distribution on a 1-D torus, 2-D Gaussian mixture, and others). There are no molecular or free-energy benchmarks. Numerics compare BDLS with N independent ULA copies at the same N; there is no tuned-competitor or wall-clock comparison. The paper also notes that pure birth-death does not enlarge the support ('the support of the solution rho_t of (5) never increases'). The method targets the full-space pi, not a CV marginal or a uniform target; that difference is correctly attributed to the project.

title: Sampling Rare Event Energy Landscapes via Birth-Death Augmented Dynamics
correct_citation: Pampel B, Holbach S, Hartung L, Valsson O. Sampling rare event energy landscapes via birth-death augmented dynamics. Phys. Rev. E 107, 024141 (2023). doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.107.024141. arXiv:2209.00607. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00607
note: The citation is correct (arXiv journal-ref: PRE 107, 024141 (2023)). The abstract (read from the v2 PDF) supports every quoted phrase. It builds on Lu-Lu-Nolen and shows the scheme 'can efficiently sample prototypical rare event energy landscapes, and that the speed of equilibration is independent of the barrier height'. It says: 'We amend a crucial shortcoming of the original algorithm that leads to incorrect sampling of barrier regions by introducing a new approximation of the birth-death term.' The original term is the kernel-smoothed log-density, so 'flaw in the kernel approximation' is a fair gloss. It also proves the convergence results still hold, says 'we investigate ways to reduce the computational effort of the sampling scheme', and extends the method to underdamped Langevin. It concludes the scheme is 'a promising method'. IMPORTANT CAVEAT that strengthens the 'does not settle' point: Sec. II states that the authors make 'the (artificial) assumption that U is known a priori' and simulate directly in the low-dimensional space. Adapting the method to an on-the-fly estimate of pi through enhanced sampling is left as future work. So there is no ABF/adaptive bias, no orthogonal degrees of freedom, and no equal-cost comparison against a tuned adaptive-bias method.

title: Accelerate Langevin Sampling with Birth-Death Process and Exploration Component
correct_citation: Tan L, Lu J. Accelerate Langevin Sampling with Birth-Death Process and Exploration Component. SIAM/ASA J. Uncertain. Quantif. 13(3):1265-1293 (2025). doi:10.1137/23M1577584. arXiv:2305.05529 (v2 3 Jun 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05529
note: The work exists. Crossref confirms the venue: SIAM/ASA JUQ 13(3), 1265-1293, published online 25 Aug 2025. The v2 PDF header spells the title 'Accelerated Langevin Sampling...', while arXiv and the journal use 'Accelerate'. VERIFIED VERBATIM (arXiv v2, p. 8, under 'Langevin sampling with birth-death process'): 'we note that d_t rho_t(x) remains zero whenever rho_t(x) itself is zero, so the support of rho_t never expand. This implies that the exploration process of BDLS solely relies on the Langevin component, which means its exploration rate cannot surpass that of pure Langevin dynamics.' Page 2 says pre-asymptotic performance 'is limited by the exploration stage', and that BDLS becomes efficient only after all modes are discovered. Page 3 says interacting-particle methods 'can transport particles inside the explored area' but their 'exploration speed is limited'. The claim is supported. Scope caveat: the argument is a mean-field statement about full-space birth-death toward pi. The paper does not discuss collective variables, marginal-only selection, hidden or orthogonal slow coordinates, or ABF. Applying it to the WCA and alanine negatives is the project's (reasonable) extrapolation, not something the paper states.

title: Exploration vs Convergence Speed in Adaptive-bias Enhanced Sampling
correct_citation: Invernizzi M, Parrinello M. Exploration vs Convergence Speed in Adaptive-Bias Enhanced Sampling. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 18(6):3988-3996 (2022). doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00152. arXiv:2201.09950. https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.09950
note: The work exists. Crossref confirms JCTC 18(6), 3988-3996, published online 26 May 2022; the given citation is correct and needs volume/issue/pages added. The arXiv abstract supports the claim. With suboptimal CVs, adaptive-bias methods face an exploration-convergence trade-off: 'one must choose between' a quickly converging bias with fewer transitions and a slower-converging bias that explores more efficiently but takes longer to give an accurate free-energy estimate. OPES prioritizes convergence, so the paper introduces a variant that prioritizes escaping metastable states (OPES-explore, implemented in PLUMED as OPES_METAD_EXPLORE). It is reported to outperform metadynamics on prototypical systems. The paper does not cover ABF or birth-death. Using it to frame what 'accelerate' means for FR is the project's own framing, but a fair one.
